newsitem.title: UK: UK minister says no need for revolt over Europe.
newsitem.headline: UK minister says no need for revolt over Europe.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind tried on Friday to head off a possible revolt over Europe by members of the ruling Conservative party, saying a mutiny would play straight into the hands of the opposition.
"The vast number of Conservative MPs are very, very reasonable people," the minister told BBC radio.

"They know perfectly well the (opposition) Labour Party are simply interested in trying to exploit any differences for opportunistic electoral reasons," he said. The next election must be held by May 1997.

Some members of parliament (MPs) threatened to withdraw support from the government after Prime Minister John Major on Thursday resisted demands for a full debate on plans for the introduction of a single European currency.

Major, with a majority of just one in parliament, has spent much of his time in power dealing with the threat posed by Eurosceptic members of parliament, who oppose any move towards European integration.

He triggered the latest unrest within Conservative ranks by refusing to give way to calls for a debate on three documents detailing how a European currency will be introduced and how countries that do not join will be treated.

Rifkind said there was no question of the government trying to suppress debate on the matter, saying parliament would have a full day to discuss European matters before a summit of EU leaders in Dublin next month.

"Of course I recognise, as does the prime minister, that a number of members of parliament would like a wider discussion. That opportunity will exist," he said, adding that the documents had already been discussed by a parliamentary committee.
"That should be sufficient, but obviously there is a lot of feeling expressed by some members of parliament. There will be a further opportunity to debate these matters...

"It will be possible for every member of parliament who wishes to, to raise these matters, and for ministers to reply to any concerns that are expressed. I think that's a very reasonable way forwards.

He also tried to play down reports that members of an influential Conservative committee had savaged the government during a meeting late on Thursday for its refusal to hold a full debate on a European currency.
"Neither you or I were at that meeting," he told the radio interviewer, saying that Major would meet Sir Marcus Fox -- chairman of the so-called 1922 committee -- next week.
Newspapers portrayed the decision as a snub, saying Fox had demanded an immediate meeting to express his concerns.
"The important point is that there has been a request for a meeting. The Prime Minister has agreed to that," Rifkind said.
The demand for a full debate came a day after the government sufferred an embarrassing defeat in the parliamentary committee where it was trying to force the regulations through.

Major is under increasing pressure after Labour's new pledge to hold a referendum before taking Britain into a single currency, with Conservatives worried at their election prospects demanding a tougher government line on Europe.
